anchor_label: complete horse skeletons with antler bridle elements
vehicle: No vehicle survived in the selected burial; a chariot or cart is inferred as part of the wider package
horses: A deliberately paired burial of two complete horses
control: Antler cheekpieces and knobs preserve bridle equipment
people: No driver or crew was interred in this selected context
upkeep: Low skeletal lesion evidence suggests care but does not quantify training or work
institution: An elite barrow incorporated paired horses and control gear into funerary display
interpretation: The paired horses and bridle elements show that adopting horse-drawn mobility involved animals and control equipment together, even where the wooden vehicle is absent.
limits: The vehicle did not survive and the authors allow chariot and/or cart use. This burial cannot establish battlefield use, a chariot force, horse-training intensity, or a regional adoption date.

anchor_label: reconstructed training days in the preserved schedule
vehicle: The text repeatedly trains horses for chariot work but does not inventory vehicles
horses: Chariot horses are the explicit subject of a long conditioning program
control: Harnessing and rounds on a training ground are prescribed within the program
people: Kikkuli is named as a specialist horse trainer; scribes preserved the instruction
upkeep: Feed and water schedules, stabling, pasture, blankets, massage, and timed exercise
institution: A specialist program was copied and retained in the royal archive at Hattusha
interpretation: A chariot horse was not ready merely because a state owned a vehicle: conditioning, feeding, care, specialist knowledge, and an archive all entered the system.
limits: At least 184 days is a scholarly reconstruction from preserved units, not an ancient numbered total. One archived instruction does not measure compliance, horse survival, force size, or comparative effectiveness.

anchor_label: recorded wheel pairs; 13 listed as unfit for service
vehicle: The Sa series inventories detachable chariot wheels rather than complete chariots
horses: Horses are not counted in the selected Sa-series observation
control: Separate harness and fittings series exist, but they are not added to this wheel tally
people: Drivers and crews are absent from the selected wheel inventory
upkeep: Serviceable and unfit wheels are distinguished; materials and condition are recorded
institution: Palatial records stored, inspected, and categorized military equipment
interpretation: A wheel inventory that marks thirteen pairs unfit for service makes maintenance visible: possessing chariots required stocks, inspection, repair, and replacement parts.
limits: The archive is fragmentary and 58 wheel pairs are not 58 complete or fieldable chariots. The record cannot recover horses, crews, annual production, repair time, or the size of a Pylian chariot force.

anchor_label: one chariot and two horses sent as a greeting gift
vehicle: Aššur-uballiṭ I explicitly sends one good chariot
horses: Two horses accompany that one vehicle
control: The letter does not itemize harness, reins, or yoke
people: A royal messenger carries the gift; no combat crew is described
upkeep: Training, fodder, transport, and repair are outside the surviving message
institution: A gift between great kings makes a complete chariot package an object of elite diplomacy
interpretation: The vehicle and its matched horse team crossed a diplomatic network as one prestigious package, not as an isolated weapon design.
limits: A diplomatic gift is not a military inventory, price, standard issue, or evidence that every chariot used exactly the same support system. The letter does not identify its itinerary or battlefield use.

anchor_label: M40: one chariot, two horses, and three people
vehicle: M40 preserves fittings and traces of box, axle, draft pole, yoke, and yoke saddles
horses: Two horses were buried with the M40 chariot
control: Horse and chariot fittings plus rein holders occur in the Anyang assemblages
people: Three people were buried in M40; other pits preserve identified charioteers
upkeep: M41 and elite graves preserve axes, chisels, and other tools interpreted for chariot woodwork repair
institution: Mortuary pits, elite graves, and local workshops embedded chariot skill in Shang ritual and warfare
interpretation: At Anyang, horses, vehicle, fittings, people, weapons, repair tools, and elite institutions appear together—the archaeological signature of a transferred knowledge package.
limits: M40 quantities and M41 repair tools come from different pits, and mortuary staging is not field organization. These finds do not give an army total, crew standard, casualty rate, or date for the first Chinese chariot.
